title: Young Founders: Building What's Next
notice: Synthetic demo material. Invented document; no real meeting, publication, email or call occurred.

blocks.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Emerald City Leadership Network’s June webinar. I’m Rowan Bell, your community manager. For those who don’t know me, I mostly work behind the scenes to keep this network connected. And today, we’re here to talk with five of our Young Founders. We’ve got Calla Thistlestead from the Junction Quarter Refill Shop, Posy Haystead from Haystead Design Studio, Jasper Gatefield from Gatefield Tutoring, Lux Thistlefield from Thistlefield Tutoring, and Reuben Spindlecombe from the Spectacle Lane Refill Shop. Thanks, all, for joining.
Let’s start with a quick round of introductions. What’s the core of what you’re building right now? Calla, maybe we can start with you.

Hi! Calla here. Right, so my shop is a refill counter in Junction Quarter. It’s simple—you bring your own jars, we fill them with oats, oil, soap, that sort of thing. I opened up a few months back. The best bit is this shelf near the door—it’s for donated jars. People leave their spare ones, and if someone forgets to bring a jar? They can just take one from the shelf. It’s a little community pantry but for containers. Keeps things moving.

Posy Haystead. I run a design studio, mostly print and layout. My project at the moment is with Gillikin Growers. I’ve just restructured their monthly member newsletter. It was a dense, single-column text wall. Now it’s a two-column digestible format. We kept the page count the same but made room for three more member profiles per issue. The first one in the new layout goes out next week.

Jasper Gatefield, Gatefield Tutoring. I focus on making math less of a mystery. For a recent project, I hosted a free geometry workshop in the Spectacle Lane library courtyard. No desks, no paper—just me, a bucket of chalk, and twenty kids. We drew right on the paving stones: triangles, parallel lines, all that. It’s like… you know when you’re trying to explain a game and it’s easier if you just get up and show the moves? That’s what the chalk was for. They got the angle properties because they could walk around the diagrams.

Lux Thistlefield, of Thistlefield Tutoring. I believe education is a shared journey! While I tutor, my current focus is building my team. I’m planning to establish a peer observation program. Imagine it: one of my tutors sits in on another’s session, just to watch, to listen, to share a technique later over tea. Not for evaluation, but for cross-pollination of ideas. I think it will lift everyone up. That’s the plan I’m working on now.

Reuben Spindlecombe, Spectacle Lane Refill Shop. We sell dry goods, liquids, cleaning supplies—all the usuals. I tried something new: dissolvable laundry pods in compostable film. Sounded perfect, right? No plastic packet. Well, the trial’s over. Our shop’s a bit humid, especially near the window. The film absorbed it, and the pods started sticking together in the dispenser. I had a few batches turn into one giant lump. It was a mess. So, that’s halted for now. Back to the drawing board on that packaging.
Thanks, everyone. That’s a great mix of what’s working and what’s… a learning experience. Let’s dig into that a bit. Reuben, when you hit that snag with the pods, what was your first move?

First move? I un-stuck the dispenser! Then I talked to my suppliers. They were surprised—said the film should’ve held up. I realized I’d need a dehumidifier in that corner to even think about trying again, and that’s an extra cost I hadn’t factored. So the first move was really just admitting the test failed and pulling the product. It’s still a good idea, just not with this material in this location.
Calla, your jar shelf is such a simple idea. Has it worked the way you hoped?

Pretty much! It’s never empty, which is the main thing. People are generous. I’ve seen a parent come in with a kid, they’d forgotten their jar, and the kid got to pick one from the shelf—a big colorful one with a old pickle label still on it. He was thrilled. It takes the pressure off. The only hiccup is sometimes I get a run on a certain size, like everyone needs a half-liter jar at once, but it balances out.
Posy, shifting that newsletter format—was that a request from Gillikin Growers, or did you propose it?

They said they wanted to feature more members but couldn’t add pages due to printing costs. I proposed the two-column layout. It’s a visual solution to a content problem. It creates more entry points on the page, so even if someone just flips through, a photo or a pull-quote might catch their eye. It’s a structural change, not just a cosmetic one.
Jasper, how did you get the word out about the chalk geometry workshop?

Flyers at the library, obviously. But also, I just told my regular students and asked them to bring a friend. It’s like when you’re planning a picnic—you tell a few people, they tell a few more, and suddenly you’ve got a crowd. Twenty felt like the right number. Any more and you can’t see the chalk from the back.
Lux, your peer observation plan is still in the works. What’s the first step to getting it off the ground?

The first step is conversation! I’m talking with each of my tutors individually, listening to their thoughts. Some are excited, some are nervous about being watched. So I’m drafting a set of guidelines—a framework that makes it feel supportive, not scrutinizing. Things like, ‘We observe one technique, not the whole person.’ And we’ll start with volunteers. It has to be built on trust.
We’ve got a question from the audience, for anyone: ‘How do you decide when to stick with an idea and when to let it go?’

I’ll jump in. With the pods, I let it go when the core promise—convenient, eco-friendly packaging—was broken. If the product is stuck together, it’s not convenient. Letting it go isn’t killing the idea forever; it’s just admitting this version doesn’t work in these conditions.

I decide based on the goal. With the newsletter, the goal was more profiles without more pages. The two-column layout met that goal. If it hadn’t, I’d have scrapped it and looked at type size or paper weight instead. You have to know what you’re solving for.

For me, if an idea makes things easier for my customers and doesn’t make a huge mess for me, I stick with it. The jar shelf passes. If it started attracting folks who just wanted free jars and never bought anything… well, I’d have to think. But so far, it’s just a nice thing.
Another audience question: ‘What’s one thing you’ve learned from another member of this network?’

I learned from talking to Posy last month about white space. Not just on a page, but in a lesson plan. Leaving room for questions, for tangents. She called it ‘visual breathing room.’ I’ve started building that into my sessions. It helps.

Calla’s jar shelf! It’s a beautiful example of low-threshold generosity. It’s not a formal program, it’s just a shelf. I’m thinking about how to apply that ‘low-threshold’ idea to my observation plan—making it easy to say yes.
Hearing Jasper talk about his chalk workshop reminded me to just try things. My pod trial failed, but at least I tried it. He just got some chalk and did it. That’s the energy I want to keep.
We’re about out of time. A final thought from each of you? One word or a short phrase on what you’re taking from today.
Keep the shelf stocked.
Structure enables content.
Draw on the ground.
Build with trust.
Un-stick and replan.
Perfect. Thank you all so much for your time and your honesty. And thank you to everyone who joined us. The recording and notes will be in the network digest next week. Have a good evening.
